![An example AVeriTeC claim with three question-answer pairs, a *Conflicting Evidence/Cherrypicking* verdict, and a textual justification explaining how the QA pairs combine into the verdict. Figure 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

In *AVeriTeC: A Dataset for Real-world Claim Verification with Evidence from the Web* [[1]](#ref-1), [Michael Schlichtkrull](https://aclanthology.org/people/michael-schlichtkrull/), [Zhijiang Guo](https://aclanthology.org/people/z/zhijiang-guo/), and [Andreas Vlachos](https://aclanthology.org/people/a/andreas-vlachos/) (Cambridge) introduce a 4,568-claim fact-checking dataset sourced from 50 real fact-checking organizations, with web-retrieved evidence structured as question-answer pairs and a 4-way verdict label that adds *Conflicting Evidence/Cherrypicking* alongside the usual *Supported / Refuted / Not Enough Evidence*.

> Existing datasets for automated fact-checking have substantial limitations, such as relying on artificial claims, lacking annotations for evidence and intermediate reasoning, or including evidence published after the claim. In this paper we introduce *AVeriTeC, a new dataset of 4,568 real-world claims covering fact-checks by 50 different organizations*. Each claim is annotated with *question-answer pairs supported by evidence available online*, as well as *textual justifications explaining how the evidence combines to produce a verdict*. Through a multi-round annotation process, we avoid common pitfalls including *context dependence, evidence insufficiency, and temporal leakage*, and reach a substantial inter-annotator agreement of $\kappa=0.619$ on verdicts. We develop *a baseline as well as an evaluation scheme for verifying claims through several question-answering steps against the open web*.

## Method

The cover figure (Figure 2 from the paper) shows the shape of one annotated example. The claim — "The USA has succeeded in reducing greenhouse emissions in previous years" (Morgan Griffith, 2020-11-02) — is decomposed into three questions: total emissions in 2007, when emissions dropped, whether they rose again after 2017. Each answer cites a specific number with a sourced URL. The verdict is *Conflicting Evidence/Cherrypicking* because the supporting evidence is real (emissions did fall) but incomplete (they rose again), and the textual justification names that gap directly. This is what every row in AVeriTeC looks like: a claim, a small set of QA pairs that together carry the evidence, a verdict, and a justification that ties the QA pairs to the verdict — closer to a fact-checker's workflow than to FEVER-style sentence retrieval.

Each claim is labelled by a five-phase pipeline: claim extraction and normalization, question-answer generation, evidence-sufficiency check, a second QA round when verdicts disagree, and a final sufficiency check. Pages used as evidence are cached in the Internet Archive to keep the test set reproducible, and the released splits are temporally ordered (train ends Aug 2020, dev ends Oct 2020, test ends Dec 2021) so a model trained on FEVER-style [[2]](#ref-2) closed-corpus retrieval can be benchmarked against a real open-web setting without rebuilding infrastructure. Each phase exists to address a specific failure mode the authors call out in earlier datasets:

- **Context dependence** — many fact-checking-derived claims (e.g. "unemployment is rising") are unverifiable without surrounding article context. The first phase has annotators rewrite each claim to be self-contained: resolving coreference, naming the speaker, locking down the time and place, before any QA work begins.
- **Evidence insufficiency** — labels in earlier datasets often don't match the annotated evidence. The second-phase annotator generates QA pairs and a tentative verdict; a *different* third-phase annotator then sees only those QA pairs (not the original article) and produces an independent verdict. Disagreement triggers a second QA round; persistent disagreement discards the claim. The "blind" sufficiency check forces evidence to stand alone.
- **Temporal leakage** — annotators search through a custom Google bar restricted to documents published before the claim date, evidence-document dates are ordered against claim dates, and the train/dev/test splits are themselves temporally disjoint so a test claim from 2021 cannot share evidence with a training claim from 2020. This is the main defense against training-time leaks where later language models would otherwise trivially "verify" historical claims.

![The five-phase annotation pipeline: claims are normalised, then question-answer generation alternates with an evidence-sufficiency check by a different annotator. Disagreement between the two verdicts triggers a second QA round; persistent disagreement discards the claim. Figure 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure1.png){fig-align="center"}

## Results

The dataset comprises 4,568 claims (3,068 train / 500 dev / 1,000 test), 2.60 questions per claim on average, label distribution dominated by Refuted (~60%) with Supported ~25%, Conflicting ~7%, Not Enough Evidence ~7%. Inter-annotator agreement is $\kappa=0.619$ (Randolph's free-marginal multirater $\kappa$, chosen because Fleiss' $\kappa$ underestimates on unbalanced data — Fleiss equivalent is $0.503$). Evaluation uses *Hungarian METEOR*, the paper's name for scoring generated QA pairs against gold ones by computing pairwise METEOR [[3]](#ref-3) similarity and then solving the optimal one-to-one assignment between generated and reference sequences with the Hungarian algorithm [[4]](#ref-4) — turning a bag-of-evidence retrieval task into a matching problem so that asking "the right question phrased differently" still gets credit. Recommended cutoff $\lambda=0.25$. Headline baseline numbers below.

| Model            | Q only | Q + A | Veracity @ λ=0.25 | Justifications @ λ=0.25 |
|------------------|--------|-------|-------------------|-------------------------|
| No search        | 0.19   | 0.11  | 0.02              | 0.01                    |
| Gold evidence    | 1.00   | 1.00  | 0.49              | 0.28                    |
| AVeriTeC-BLOOM-7b| 0.26   | 0.21  | 0.15              | 0.07                    |
| gpt-3.5-turbo    | 0.29   | 0.16  | 0.10              | 0.04                    |

: AVeriTeC baseline (BLOOM-7b pipeline) versus a no-search ablation, an oracle that uses gold QA pairs as evidence, and `gpt-3.5-turbo` generating evidence and verdicts directly. Retrieval is scored with Hungarian METEOR; veracity and justification scores are accuracy and METEOR, conditioned on retrieving correct evidence at $\lambda=0.25$. Table 3 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).

The four columns score two different things:

- **Q only** — Hungarian METEOR over generated vs. gold question strings alone. Does the model ask the right thing?
- **Q + A** — Hungarian METEOR over each question concatenated with its answer. Does the model ask the right thing *and* find the right answer?
- **Veracity @ λ=0.25** — verdict accuracy, but a claim only scores if its retrieved evidence cleared $\lambda=0.25$ on Q+A. A wrong-evidence claim gets 0 even when the verdict happens to be correct, which is the design choice that makes "Gold evidence" the practical ceiling at 0.49 rather than 1.0.
- **Justifications @ λ=0.25** — METEOR between generated and gold justifications, conditioned on the same evidence-retrieval gate.

The four rows bracket the system between two limits and add two real configurations:

- **No search** — gives the model nothing and uses BERT-large to predict the verdict from the claim alone. A lower bound that isolates how much can be guessed from claim wording (about 17% macro-F1 per Table 4, dominated by the *Refuted* class prior).
- **Gold evidence** — feeds the annotators' QA pairs to the verdict-prediction and justification-generation heads (BERT-large + a prompted language model) as if retrieval were solved. An upper bound that isolates those downstream components from retrieval noise.
- **AVeriTeC-BLOOM-7b** — the full pipeline: BLOOM-7b (prompted with 10 in-context examples retrieved from the training set, no fine-tuning) generates search-query questions, Google + BM25 retrieve passages, a fine-tuned BERT-large re-ranker selects the best passages, BLOOM-7b generates one question per surviving passage to recover Q+A pairs, a second fine-tuned BERT-large does stance detection to decide the verdict, and a fine-tuned BART-large writes the justification. The "BLOOM-7b" label names only the in-context question-generator slot — the authors also tried Vicuna-13b there and report BLOOM winning, attributed to more diverse questions.
- **gpt-3.5-turbo** — skips retrieval entirely and prompts ChatGPT to produce verdict, evidence, and justification end-to-end. Useful as a fluency upper bound but prone to fabricating sources.

The 0.34-point gap between the gold-evidence and AVeriTeC-BLOOM-7b veracity scores is the paper's clearest signal: even with a competent verdict head, the bottleneck is retrieval. ChatGPT outperforms the baseline on bare question generation but loses on the AVeriTeC score because its generated "evidence" often hallucinates sources that look plausible but cannot be matched to gold answers. The authors give an example: ChatGPT correctly verdicts a vitamin-K claim *Supported* while inventing a USDA citation that doesn't exist.

## My Notes

- **AVeriTeC freezes the gold side of the benchmark but not the retrieval side, a structural flaw for fair cross-system comparison.** The reproducibility mechanism the paper proposes (Internet Archive snapshots of the *gold* evidence pages) keeps the answers re-fetchable, but it does not freeze the *retrieval setup* a baseline searches. Baselines hit live Google, and two systems run a year apart see different rankings, different page contents at the same URL, and newly-indexed pages, so cross-time and cross-system score deltas drift with the web rather than with the system. The temporal-leakage protection has the same shape: annotator search is filtered to documents Google reports as published before the claim date (itself an estimate), but for any modern LLM whose pretraining cutoff is past 2021-12-22, the entire test set is in-distribution and the date guarantee is moot. The FEVER 2024 shared task closed both gaps by providing a "knowledge store" snapshot every system retrieves from instead of live Google, which is the right design, but it's a shared-task addition rather than part of the original paper. Anyone using AVeriTeC for new top-line numbers needs that knowledge store (or a re-collection of newer claims), or the comparisons are not measuring what they look like.
- **AVeriTeC's distinctness comes from five ingredients combined, not any one alone.** Real-world claims (vs FEVER-style synthetic), web-retrieved evidence (vs closed Wikipedia corpus), QA-pair decomposition of that evidence (vs flat sentence retrieval), a textual justification per claim (vs none), and a four-way label set including *Conflicting Evidence/Cherrypicking* (vs three labels). Prior benchmarks have at most two of these. FEVER [[2]](#ref-2) is Wikipedia-derived synthetic claims with three labels, flat sentence evidence, no justifications. MultiFC [[5]](#ref-5) has real claims but no usable evidence annotation, no QA structure, no justifications. HoVer [[6]](#ref-6) keeps Wikipedia retrieval and adds multi-hop, but still flat sentences and three labels. The *Conflicting Evidence/Cherrypicking* class adds the most substance: fact-checkers spend a real share of their time on technically-true-but-misleading claims that don't fit *Supported* or *Refuted*, and a benchmark with no class for them quietly trains models to force a choice.
- **Hungarian METEOR has a noise floor, and the system sits on it.** Two annotators redoing the same claim only agree at 0.28 on questions and 0.22 on questions+answers. AVeriTeC-BLOOM-7b scores 0.21 on Q+A, *at* the annotator-agreement floor; ChatGPT scores 0.16, similarly below. The paper traces the low agreement to two causes: different annotators reaching the same verdict via different evidence paths, and phrasing equivalent QA pairs differently. METEOR penalises both even though the underlying annotation is correct.
  - For the paraphrase cause, trained semantic-similarity scoring (BLEURT [[7]](#ref-7), BERTScore, or an LLM-judge with a calibrated equivalence rubric) replaces n-gram overlap with meaning equivalence. The paper itself recommends BLEURT; an LLM-judge is the more current upgrade.
  - For the divergent-evidence-path cause, the paper sketches a max-over-references extension: collect multiple gold QA-pair sets per claim and score against the best match. A complementary move is *verdict-conditional* scoring — give credit when the model reaches the right verdict via any valid evidence path with sourced answers, decoupling evidence-string match from verdict correctness. The retrieval-side score still punishes hallucinated sources, so the abstention/factuality property the paper cares about isn't lost.
  - The gold-evidence row at 1.00 is uninformative as a ceiling here, since by construction it returns the gold strings. Until one of these remedies is in place, system-vs-system retrieval deltas in the low hundredths on AVeriTeC are mostly metric noise, not real differences.
- **AVeriTeC's NEI label rewards weak retrieval as if it were calibrated abstention.** A model with bad retrieval will frequently fail to find supporting evidence even on claims that *are* supportable, and the natural prediction in that state is *Not Enough Evidence*. On the truly-NEI portion of the test set, those predictions get full credit; across the rest of the test set, they get partial credit by coincidence. Both forms of credit look like the model "knew when to abstain", but neither involves the model assessing its own confidence — it just retrieved badly. This matters because *selective prediction* (the setting where a system can decline to answer when uncertain) needs the abstention signal to be a property of *the model*: low confidence in its own output, not low evidence in the world. AVeriTeC's NEI conflates the two. The gold label means *annotators could not find evidence on the open web*, which is a property of the claim and the world. Anyone using this dataset for selective-prediction or calibration work (e.g. an extension of [Conformal Factuality](/posts/20260505-conformal-factuality/) [[8]](#ref-8)) needs an *explicit* abstain channel separate from the four-way label, scored against the model's own confidence calibration. Reusing the gold NEI class as the abstention target produces apparent calibration that is really retrieval failure.
